Bangladesh confirms deal to buy Chinese J-10 fighter jets: report. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has confirmed a deal to purchase China’s 4.5-generation J-10CE fighter jets, citing the aircraft’s reported combat performance against French-made Rafale jets during the brief Pakistan-India conflict in May, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported on Friday.

The Chengdu J-10C is a single-engine, multirole combat aircraft manufactured in China. Boasting a top speed of Mach 1.8, it can be fitted with a variety of air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions. It played a key role on the first night of hostilities, shooting down six jets belonging to the Indian Air Force.

The Information and Broadcasting Adviser to the Prime Minister of Bangladesh Zahedur Rahman said earlier this week that a draft proposal to buy the jets had been submitted to the country’s finance ministry and Armed Forces Division for final approval, SCMP reported citing the Bangladeshi Press Information Department (PID).

According to the Bangladesh PID, the draft proposal also includes the purchase of Chinese attack helicopters, VIP transport helicopters and drones.

“Subject to necessary budgetary allocation in the current fiscal year, this procurement will be executed immediately; otherwise, it will roll over into the next budget cycle,” it added.

SCMP reports that Rahman said Bangladesh “paid attention” to the war last year, when Pakistan used J-10 fighters and PL-15 long-range air-to-air missiles to shoot down Indian Rafales.

In January this year, Pakistan and Bangladesh’s air chiefs held detailed discussions on the “potential procurement” of the locally-produced JF-17 Thunder aircraft, according to Inter-Services Public Relations.

It added that Bangladesh Air Force Air Chief Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan called on Pakistan Air Force Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Babar Sidhu in Islamabad, where “The meeting focused on strengthening operational cooperation and institutional synergy, with emphasis on training, capacity building, and collaboration in aerospace advancements.”

A day later, Dhaka’s air chief discussed avenues for enhancing defence cooperation with Pakistan in separate meetings with Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf.

A year ago, Pakistan was engaged in a military conflict with India, dealing the boastful neighbour an internationally recognised “clear setback”.

The conflict with India, starting from the April 22 Pahalgam attack to the end of Operation Bunyanum Marsoos, with a ceasefire ending a military escalation between the two countries on May 10, has been called “Marka-i-Haq” (Battle of Truth) by the state.

But from the night of May 6 to May 10, the drums of war were echoing loudly across South Asia as the nuclear-armed arch-rivals exchanged missiles, raising global alarm over the risk of unpredictable escalation.

item.title: Narrow-mindedness cannot police our culture. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent Dhaka Tribune report asked a very salient question: “Who gets to decide what Bangladesh can celebrate?” It is a question that goes to the heart of a troubling pattern that cannot and must not be ignored.
What cannot be denied is that increasingly, cultural events across the country are being challenged, curtailed, or cancelled because a vocal minority claims offense, threatens disruption, or insists that their interpretation of faith should dictate public life.
This policing of culture is not only unacceptable but dangerous. Such policing chips away at the secular, pluralistic foundations on which our nation was built.
Bangladesh’s cultural identity has always been expansive. We have traditions that long predate the modern state, and such diversity has given us our richness and resilience.
Yet recent years have seen a steady rise in attempts to narrow that identity -- to declare certain music, festivals, or performances “un‑Islamic,” to intimidate organizers, and to pressure authorities into cancellations.
What is most disappointing is when the state yields to such pressure, thereby sending a dangerous message: That loud threats can override lawful expression and intolerance can dictate public policy.
Bangladesh cannot afford this slide. A nation that allows cultural policing to flourish risks losing the very soul of its identity.
Secularism in Bangladesh was never meant to erase religion but meant to ensure that no single group could impose its worldview. Pluralism was never ornamental but a promise that Bangladesh belonged to all its people, regardless of faith, tradition, or cultural practice.
The incidents highlighted in recent times, from disrupted concerts to cancelled festivals, show how fragile that promise has become.
A confident nation does not fear its own culture and it does not silence its own traditions. We must reclaim that confidence.
We must stop capitulating to intimidation and make something clear: Bangladesh’s cultural space is not up for negotiation.

item.title: Extreme heat is climate injustice. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent finding that 22 million Bangladeshi children are now exposed to intensified heat should alarm every policy-maker in the country.
Extreme heat is no longer an abstract climate concern but a direct, daily threat to our children’s health, development, and future.
As one of the world’s most heat‑vulnerable nations, the fact that our children are paying the price for a crisis they did nothing to create should anger us deeply.
Heat affects children differently and more severely, increasing the risk of dehydration, respiratory distress, malnutrition, and long‑term developmental harm. It disrupts schooling, reduces outdoor play, and places enormous stress on families who must navigate rising temperatures without adequate cooling, shade, or healthcare access.
Protecting children from heat thus requires year‑round planning: Better heat‑resilient school infrastructure, shaded community spaces, early‑warning systems, and public health campaigns that help families recognize and respond to heat stress. Our urban planning must also recognize the importance of tree cover and ventilation.
With that said, while Bangladesh must do all it can to combat the effects of climate-change induced heat, it should not be shouldering this burden alone.
It bears repeating that wealthy nations have contributed to the climate crisis, yet it is countries like Bangladesh that bear the brunt of the consequences.
Protecting vulnerable children thereby requires climate finance that is predictable, adequate, and accessible. Grants - not loans - must support adaptation measures and technology transfers must be real, not rhetorical. Global climate negotiations must also stop sidelining the needs of heat‑exposed children in the Global South, treating them as if their concerns are secondary.
Bangladesh is doing what it can, but the scale of the crisis demands international responsibility. No child should suffer because the world’s richest countries failed to act time and time again.

Safety in the Rohingya camps must be ensured. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The killing of a five‑year‑old child in the Rohingya camps is a devastating reminder of how precarious life has become for those who sought refuge in Bangladesh.
The camps in Cox’s Bazar were meant to offer temporary safety to a population fleeing genocide and persecution. Instead, they have increasingly become sites of danger -- from landslides and fires to criminal violence and structural failures.
A child’s death under such circumstances therefore can no longer be simply dismissed as an accident but rather be seen as evidence of a system under severe strain.
Overcrowding, fragile terrain, and shrinking international aid have created conditions where even basic safety cannot be guaranteed. This was never supposed to be the situation in these camps.
Children, who make up a large share of the camp population, are the most vulnerable. When a retaining wall collapses or violence erupts, they are the ones who suffer first.
Bangladesh has shown extraordinary generosity by hosting more than a million Rohingya refugees -- this is an irrefutable fact. However, generosity alone does not ensure protection.
Camp safety must be treated as a core humanitarian priority, and Bangladesh cannot and must not be expected to shoulder this responsibility alone.
The need for stronger policing and community engagement is undeniable to prevent violence and protect the most vulnerable, yet this strengthening will not be possible under present circumstances.
International responsibility therefore is critical to ensuring that the situation doesn’t take a turn for the worse. Funding cuts have already reduced food rations, education services, and infrastructure maintenance.
A camp system starved of resources cannot keep people safe. Donor fatigue is not an excuse when children’s lives are at stake.
Safety in the Rohingya camps must be ensured -- with the seriousness every human life deserves.

item.title: Standing besides Nepal. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With flash floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border causing widespread destruction, once again we have learned just how vulnerable Himalayan communities can be to sudden and extreme natural events.
The recent devastating disaster that struck Nepal has left hundreds dead, many more missing, and communities across the country grappling with unimaginable loss.
At this moment of profound distress, Bangladesh’s offer of assistance to Nepal is both appropriate and commendable. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman have expressed solidarity with the Nepalese people and government, while making clear that it is prepared to assist in relief and rescue operations.
It is imperative, now, that this solidarity does not remain confined to words. Bangladesh must stand ready to translate its offer into practical assistance as soon as Nepal identifies its needs.
Whether that means medical teams, emergency supplies, rescue personnel, logistical support, or other forms of humanitarian aid, Dhaka should respond swiftly and generously wherever it can.
Bangladesh itself is no stranger to the devastation caused by floods, landslides, and other natural disasters, and this experience gives us an especially important understanding of what Nepal is going through.
It also gives us an opportunity to demonstrate the spirit of regional cooperation that South Asia so often needs, but too rarely sees in practice.
The scale of the tragedy also warrants a broader international response. Nepal should not have to confront such a catastrophe alone, particularly when rescue operations are complicated by damaged infrastructure and difficult terrain.
Bangladesh should use its diplomatic channels, including regional and multilateral forums, to encourage greater international assistance.
Natural disasters know no borders, but neither should humanitarian compassion. Bangladesh has a responsibility to stand beside a friendly neighbour during its darkest hour.
Our assistance, however modest, can help save lives, ease suffering, and remind the people of Nepal that they are not alone.
It's time to offer solidarity in the form of real, effective action.

item.title: The evolution of nationalism and the 'Bangladesh first' doctrine. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh emerged in 1971 through an emancipatory nationalism rooted in Bengali language, culture, democratic representation, and resistance to economic exploitation. Bengali nationalism supplied the moral energy of liberation.
Sovereignty, however, transformed the central political question. The issue was no longer only how Bengalis could achieve self-determination, but how the new republic could include every citizen, including communities that did not identify ethnically as Bengali.
This problem appeared during constitution-making when the citizenry was defined as Bengali. Manabendra Narayan Larma’s historic objection in the Constituent Assembly challenged the assimilation of peoples possessing their own languages, customs, and ancestral histories. His intervention exposed the distinction between cultural identity and constitutional citizenship.
The republic has since continued to negotiate the relationship between Bangalee cultural identity and Bangladeshi legal identity. In theoretical terms, this is the tension between an ethnocultural nation and a civic nation.
It was within this setting that Ziaur Rahman articulated Bangladeshi nationalism. Its principal innovation was to relocate national identity from exclusive ethnocultural markers to territorial sovereignty, citizenship, and common political destiny.
Citizens were united not by identical lineage or language, but by membership in an independent republic. The formulation emphasized territorial integrity, multiparty democracy, national production, rural development, cultural distinctiveness, and an independent foreign policy.
It sought to distinguish the sovereign identity of Bangladesh from the wider cultural geography of the Bengali-speaking world and to create an umbrella under which different ethnic and religious communities could coexist.
Begum Khaleda Zia inherited this tradition under different conditions. Her leadership against autocratic rule and the 1991 restoration of parliamentary government demonstrated that Bangladeshi nationalism could operate through electoral legitimacy.
It became associated with parliamentary politics, economic liberalization, export-led growth, and female education. Nevertheless, a winner-takes-all culture of boycotts, distrust, and executive control persisted. Tarique Rahman’s politics and the 31-Point State Reform Outline emerged as a response to this institutional crisis.
“Bangladesh first” may be understood as both a nationalist commitment and a doctrine of governance. Its central claim is that Bangladesh’s welfare, dignity, sovereignty, and decision-making autonomy must guide domestic policy and foreign relations.
This is not necessarily isolationism or autarky. It resembles strategic autonomy: International engagement remains indispensable, but partnerships must be assessed according to reciprocity, sustainability, and national interest.
In this sense, sovereignty is not withdrawal from the world; it is the capacity to engage the world without surrendering independent judgment.
The doctrine’s most important normative possibility lies in civic nationalism. Political membership should arise from equal citizenship, constitutional loyalty, and participation in common institutions -- not religious affiliation, ethnicity, or inherited status.
Accordingly, the language of merely “protecting minorities” should give way to the republican obligation to enforce universal rights. Minorities must not depend on majority benevolence. Their security, worship, dignity and political participation are enforceable constitutional entitlements.
Hannah Arendt’s famous phrase, “the right to have rights,” captures the point: Meaningful citizenship requires institutions that make rights real.
Formal equality, however, is insufficient where poverty prevents citizens from accessing food, healthcare, housing, and education. TH Marshall’s theory of social citizenship explains why civil and political rights must be accompanied by social rights.
From this perspective, the proposed Family Card and Health Card can be interpreted not as charity but as instruments of substantive citizenship.
They seek to protect low-income households, reduce food insecurity, expand primary healthcare, and strengthen maternal and child services.
Their legitimacy will depend on universal rules, transparent eligibility, and independent oversight. If distributed through partisan networks, welfare becomes clientelism; if administered through law, it can reinforce civic solidarity.
Cultural pluralism is equally necessary. Bengali language, literature, and the Liberation War remain foundational, but national culture also includes Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Garo, Santal, Manipuri, and other histories.
Unity creates a shared constitutional future; coercive uniformity produces alienation. A pluralist “Bangladesh first” must protect minority languages, include diverse histories in education, prosecute communal violence, and treat all religious and indigenous festivals as elements of the national inheritance.
The doctrine also advances a form of decentralized developmental nationalism. Political sovereignty remains fragile when economic life depends excessively on external finance, imported technology, a narrow export base, and extreme administrative centralization.
Economic sovereignty does not mean protectionist retreat; it means developing domestic capabilities so that global integration occurs from a position of resilience. Agricultural modernization, industrial diversification, technical education, and local production are therefore connected to national autonomy.
Decentralization is crucial. The principle of subsidiarity holds that decisions should be taken at the lowest effective level. Predictable fiscal transfers, elected local institutions, and participatory budgeting could enable communities to address local needs, reduce pressure on Dhaka and deepen participation beyond national elections.
Human-capital development is another pillar. Technical and vocational education in information technology, renewable energy, logistics, and healthcare can move Bangladesh beyond informal work and low-wage manufacturing.
Overseas employment should shift toward certified professional mobility, while diplomatic missions provide legal and emergency support. Citizen-centred nationalism must protect Bangladeshis wherever they work.
The doctrine returns to the Liberation War’s promises of equality, dignity, democracy, and social justice. Its ethic of “service over conflict” seeks to transform politics from a struggle for spoils into public responsibility and civic virtue.
Yet, party-based service must remain voluntary and non-partisan, never replacing the state or controlling public benefits. Internal accountability and zero tolerance for corruption and violence are indispensable.
The 31-Point Outline translates these values into institutional design. Prime-ministerial term limits seek to prevent personalized executive dominance. A bicameral legislature could widen deliberation by incorporating regional representation and specialized knowledge. Reform of Article 70 could allow members of Parliament greater independence on ordinary legislation while preserving stability on budgets and confidence votes.
Judicial independence, an effective Election Commission, an autonomous Anti-Corruption Commission, a National Ombudsman and a merit-based civil service are elements of what constitutional theory calls horizontal accountability: State institutions checking other state institutions.
John Rawls wrote that “justice is the first virtue of social institutions.” Institutional reform is therefore not an administrative luxury; it is the condition under which public power becomes legitimate.
In foreign affairs, “Bangladesh first” rests on strategic autonomy, reciprocal realism, and sovereign equality. Relations with India require cooperation on trade, borders and equitable water sharing without compromising national interests.
Chinese investment should satisfy transparency, debt-sustainability, and local employment tests. Ties with the United States and European Union remain essential for trade and technology, while partnerships with Turkey and the Islamic world can support energy, defense and action on the Rohingya crisis.
Several tensions nevertheless require vigilance.
Majority heritage must never dilute minority equality; national unity must not be used to silence opposition, journalists, academics, or peaceful protest. Support for domestic industry must not become protection for politically connected monopolies.
Constitutional amendments alone cannot change political conduct. Most importantly, the doctrine must be judged through measurable outcomes: Minority-security data, healthcare coverage, poverty reduction, youth employment, judicial independence, local-government capacity, corruption control, and electoral transparency.
Karl Popper’s idea of the open society is pertinent: Democratic strength lies in the capacity to correct policy through criticism rather than suppress criticism in the name of unity.
The movement from Bengali nationalism to Bangladeshi nationalism and then to “Bangladesh first” reflects changing stages of nation-building. Bengali nationalism generated liberation; Bangladeshi nationalism supplied a territorial civic identity; Tarique Rahman’s doctrine seeks to carry that tradition into institutional reform and developmental governance.
Its ultimate value will depend not on slogans but on the quality of citizenship it creates. A strong nation is one in which families possess social security, farmers receive fair prices, young people acquire useful skills, local communities share power, minorities worship without fear, Parliament restrains the executive, and diplomacy protects sovereignty without producing isolation.
Properly interpreted, “Bangladesh first” places neither the state above the citizen nor the majority above the minority. It places human dignity, constitutional equality, accountable institutions, and the collective welfare of the people above partisan advantage -- and thereby offers a possible ethics of democratic statecraft.
Prof Dr Saiful Islam is a political analyst and teaches at the University of Dhaka.

item.title: The gas crisis is also an accountability crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When 171 factories in Habiganj Industrial Park shut down on a single day and one and a half lakh workers go home without wages, it is no longer an energy issue. It has become a national livelihood issue.
The report published on August 28 claiming that Bangladesh had to buy LNG at $22.35 per unit on the spot market while the contract price was around $9 to $10.40, and that an extra Tk500 crore was spent for just three days of gas, has shocked many.
Whether the exact figure of Tk500 crore is precise or not, the underlying pain is real. Anyone who visited Gazipur, Narayanganj, and Savar-Ashulia in the last two weeks will confirm -- looms are silent, dyeing machines are cold, and export orders are being cancelled.
As concerned citizens, we should not get trapped in the debate of who said what. The right question is: Is this true, and what should we do about it?
Three facts are undeniable.
First, our dependency
Almost 37% of our daily gas now comes from two floating terminals in Maheshkhali. This is not a diversified energy mix; this is a single point of failure.
When one ship of Excelerate Energy caught fire on July 21, the whole industrial belt from Habiganj to Narayanganj felt the tremor. A country of 170 million people cannot afford to keep its industrial future hanging on two rented ships.
Second, the contract model
The build-operate-transfer model with a daily capacity charge of $454,000, payable even when no gas is supplied, is unusual in any competitive market. The logic of capacity charge exists worldwide, but it must be paired with heavy penalties for non-supply and strict performance guarantees.
We, the public, still do not know what those guarantees are. The 2016 contract was signed for 15 years. The ship hired was built in 2005. By the time we own it in 2032, it will be 27 years old -- effectively scrap in marine engineering terms. Who approved this asset valuation? On what basis?
Third, the planning failure
If it is true that Qatar informed as early as March that it would supply 20 cargoes instead of 40, what did Petrobangla and the energy division do for five months?
Why was there no contingency? Why was a spot purchase needed at double the price in August?
Even if there was no corruption, this is a textbook case of poor planning that costs the exchequer hundreds of crores.
This is where the citizen's stand must be clear and non-partisan.
We are not interested in scoring political points against any individual. Personalization of the crisis actually helps the system hide. If we make it about one person, the system that allowed such a contract to be signed remains untouched. The next government can do the same with a different person.
What we should demand is institutional reform.
One, full disclosure. The government must explore and publish the full contracts of both FSRU terminals -- Excelerate and Summit -- on the Petrobangla website. Not a summary, but the full contract including capacity charge, O&M charge, termination clause, and insurance liability in case of fire or accident. Let energy experts, journalists, and citizens read it.
Two, an independent energy audit. Not an internal committee of Petrobangla. A panel comprising an international LNG procurement expert, a chartered accountant, and a retired Supreme Court judge should audit all LNG spot purchases from January to August 2026. How much was bought, at what price, from whom, and who authorized it? The report must be public within 60 days.
Three, cost pass-through protection for small industries. Large groups like BSRM can absorb a few days of closure, but a small dyeing factory in Madhabdi or a weaving factory in Sirajganj cannot. Every day of closure pushes them towards becoming a loan defaulter. Bangladesh Bank must issue a special forbearance for gas-crisis-affected industries. We must also ensure that the extra cost of emergency LNG is not directly passed on to small industrial consumers.
Four, long-term correction. We must not repeat the same mistake. The permanent solution to the gas crisis is not more expensive LNG terminals.
It is:
The most painful part of this crisis is the human cost that is not visible in the $22.35 figure. In the fisheries sector alone, reports say fish worth Tk15 crore died because aerators could not run without gas-based electricity.
In a household, a mother cannot cook. In a factory, a worker earning Tk12,000 a month does not get paid if there is no production. This is the real looting -- the looting of hope.
As citizens, our stand should not be "pro-Awami League" or "pro-Pinaki." Our stand should be pro-transparency.
If the allegation of Tk500 crore looting is false, the government can prove it by publishing invoices. If it is true, the money must be recovered and those responsible must face trial, regardless of how powerful they are.
The gas crisis has given us a rare window. For the first time, people are asking questions about capacity charges, FSRU contracts, and spot market purchases -- topics that were once confined to closed-door meetings. We must not waste this window by turning it into a Facebook fight.
Let us demand documents, not slogans. Let us demand audit, not abuse. Let us demand energy security, not political revenge.
That is the only way to ensure that in August 2027, we are not writing another op-ed about another gas crisis.
Brig Gen Qazi Abidus Samad, ndc, psc (retd) is a freelance contributor.

item.description:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday said that the recent Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan had brought the three countries “closer together” and sent a message of “unity and peace throughout the region”.

​​​​​​​The three countries signed the joint defence agreement at a trilateral summit in Makkah on August 7, pledging to strengthen collective security, deepen defence cooperation and promote peace and stability in the region and beyond.

According to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), PM Shehbaz made the remarks during a meeting with Saudi Minister for Environment, Water and Agriculture Abdulrahman bin Abdulmohsen Al-Fadley at the Prime Minister’s House in Islamabad.

In a statement, the PMO said the premier reaffirmed the “deep-rooted, fraternal ties” between the two countries and conveyed his regards for King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud.

He underscored that as strategic partners, both Pakistan and the kingdom must now focus their energies towards “deepening economic and agriculture ties to translate their longstanding relationship into a stronger, mutually beneficial trade and investment partnership”.

PM Shehbaz also expressed satisfaction at the “constructive engagement” between the two sides, particularly with regard to the export of agricultural products by Pakistan to the kingdom, the statement said.

“Both sides also exchanged views on enhancing agricultural productivity in Pakistan, through the use of technology, research and development and more efficient use of water resources,” the statement added.

The premier also announced that a delegation of agricultural experts from Pakistan would soon visit Riyadh to carry forward these discussions “with a view to realise the full potential of this partnership”.

Meanwhile, the Saudi minister thanked PM Shehbaz for the warm hospitality extended to him and his delegation and reaffirmed the kingdom’s commitment to deepening cooperation with Pakistan across the agriculture, water and food security sectors, the statement concluded.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during a summit at Al-Safa Palace.

The tripartite pact empowers member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them, and reflects their “shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond, in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future”.

Pakistan has said that the pact is “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles.

On Thursday, Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said the country would consider joining the pact “positively” if invited by the founding members.

item.title: Moving beyond Dhaka’s shadow. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dhaka stands as the undisputed epicentre of Bangladesh, concentrating within its own boundaries an overwhelming share of the nation’s chances, institutions, and essential services. U niversities, advanced medical facilities, key government ministries, corporate headquarters, and big financial institutions are all in the capital.
I n contrast, district and divisional towns increasingly look mostly abandoned, left out. Their economies stay stagnant, infrastructure lags, and even more, a steady stream of eager young people migrate to Dhaka for a better future.
This lopsided development pattern has turned the capital into a magnet that pulls resources from every corner of the country, while the outer areas get weakened and not properly served.
Every year hundreds of thousands of migrants show up, mainly because comparable opportunities elsewhere are in short supply, or just don’t exist.
This hyper concentration exacts a profound toll on both the capital and the nation. Dhaka’s roads and its public transport systems buckle daily under unbearable traffic congestion, wasting countless productive hours. Housing prices have climbed way past the reach of ordinary citizens, pushing many into overcrowded slums or informal settlements with minimal basic services.
Air pollution often reaches hazardous levels, posing serious threats to public health. Water supply and waste management systems struggle to keep up, while green spaces are shrinking rapidly. These pressures not only reduce the quality of life for residents, but also gradually erode the very attractiveness that once made Dhaka the preferred destination.
The consequences extend well beyond the city limits. A student from Barishal or a patient from Rangpur often faces arduous journeys, lengthy delays, and significant expenses to access quality higher education or specialized healthcare. Government services, business registrations, and even routine administrative approvals frequently require travel to or coordination through Dhaka, breeding inefficiency and frustration.
Talented professionals in fields such as medicine, engineering, teaching, and public administration show reluctance to serve in regional postings. They know that career advancement, superior schools for their children, and access to modern amenities remain overwhelmingly centred in the capital. As a result, smaller towns experience a steady brain drain that further stifles local innovation and growth.
Regional inequality seems to get worse, year after year. You can see it clearly in higher poverty levels, weaker education results in some places, and uneven access to electricity, sanitation, and even digital connectivity.
As this goes on, whole communities end up losing their most skilled people, and that quietly erodes local administration as well as economic energy. In the end, the country pays for it -- through human potential that stays unused and chances for broader, more inclusive progress that never quite happen.
Decentralization represents far more than a policy preference and stands as the only sustainable pathway to address these structural distortions. By genuinely transferring administrative, financial, and decision-making authority to divisional and district levels, Bangladesh can begin to distribute opportunities more equitably and alleviate the unsustainable load on Dhaka.
International stories provide valuable instruction. Countries in Southeast Asia and constituents in Europe demonstrate how devolved power, coupled with robust accountability mechanisms, can unleash capacity without sacrificing country-wide coordination.
Bangladesh, with its massive youth population and growing financial system, has the demographic to replicate such success. What remains critical is regular political commitment and effective implementation.
Some observers express the position that decentralization can lead to coordination problems, poor oversight, or adjacent capacity agility. These are valid points, but the status quo is not working, gripped with severe bottlenecks, bureaucratic delays, and coordination screw-ups on a nationwide scale.
The answer is pairing decentralization with capacity-building programs for neighbourhood administrations, transparent performance-based investments, strengthened oversight frameworks and anti-corruption safeguards.
The benefits would be far-reaching. An additional balanced cityscape will reduce environmental pressures, enhance the livability among us, and allow every citizen the chance to succeed no matter the place of birth.
Reduced migration can help the social fabric in rural and small metropolitan clusters, and inject clean dynamism into local economies. Strong nearby governance can also enhance responsiveness to climate challenges, which disproportionately affect different parts of the nation.
Continued over-reliance on a single, overburdened metropolis alongside the neglect of vast regional potential is neither desirable nor tenable in the long run. The evidence from population trends, economic data, and lived experiences all point in one direction. There is simply no viable alternative to genuine decentralization.
Md Ashikur Rahman is a development worker, and a graduate and postgraduate in public administration and governance studies.

item.title: Business schools need AI. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In Bangladesh, generative AI in business education is no longer a foreign trend arriving from North American campuses -- it's already in classrooms, WhatsApp groups, assignment drafts, and student presentations.
The real question isn't whether business schools should allow AI, but whether it will produce sharper thinkers or simply faster submitters.
The numbers frame why these matters. Bangladesh had 135.94 million internet subscribers as of June 2026 (BTRC), with 120.84 million connecting via mobile rather than fixed broadband.
Household internet access rose from 43.6% (2023) to 54.8% (2025); smartphone adoption climbed from 63.3% to 72.8% over the same period (BBS).
That's real progress, but a meaningful share of any classroom remains under-connected. Classroom capacity compounds this: UGC data puts Jagannath University's teacher-student ratio near 1:25 against an international benchmark of 1:20, while several Dhaka University departments routinely exceed 40-50 students per section.
Used well, AI can help a student unpack a dense case study in plain Bangla-English, rehearse a pitch, or organize field-interview questions in advance.
Bangladesh already has strong homegrown cases for this -- bKash reached roughly 84 million verified users by 2026; the country's mobile financial services processed an estimated 8.61% of global daily mobile money transactions in 2024 despite holding just 2.19% of the world's population.
Pathao reports over 600,000 jobs created (a company figure, not independently audited); ShopUp serves small neighborhood shops through commerce and logistics support.
But the line between support and substitution is everything.
Using AI to understand why bKash succeeded is learning. Submitting an AI-written assignment without field observation is outsourcing.
The distinction determines whether the tool builds capability or erodes it.
Adoption data shows this isn't evenly distributed. One study found ChatGPT usage among Bangladeshi students rising from 5% (2022) to 49% (2025), with a stark urban-rural gap: 78% versus 32%.
That overall figure still trails the roughly 71% global higher-education adoption rate reported by 2023-2024, suggesting Bangladeshi classrooms are unevenly saturated rather than over-saturated.
The stakes extend past grades.
ICT service exports reached $724.6 million in FY2024-25 (EPB), up 7.7% year-on-year, and Bangladesh hosts an estimated 650,000 active freelancers -- among the largest online-labour workforces globally per Oxford Internet Institute research.
The draft National AI Policy 2026-2030 explicitly directs education systems to guard against over-reliance, so students keep building core reasoning skills.
Assessment design should adapt accordingly: Pairing written work with vivas, reflection logs, field evidence, and AI-use declarations reward thinking over formatting.
Faculty need institutional support to make this shift, given already-stretched teacher-student ratios. Encouragingly, Brac University's 2026 cohort sent roughly 700 students into GCI World, a global AI education initiative spanning 114 countries, a sign infrastructure investment is underway, though it alone won't solve the assessment problem.
Bangladesh doesn't need graduates who submit just polished paragraphs but who can reason through messy realities. AI must be a tool for asking better questions, not skipping the struggle of answering them.
Dr Nusrat Hafiz is an Assistant Professor and Director, Women Empowerment Cell, Brac Business School, Brac University.

item.title: A record 129 failures: The agonizing timeline of the Sagar-Runi probe. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Investigating agencies in Bangladesh failed for a record 129th time yesterday to submit the probe report for the sensational double murder case involving the gruesome 2012 killing of journalist couple Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi inside the safety of their Dhaka home.
The incident immediately hogged the media spotlight and has never faded from public memory, particularly because the home minister at the time promised on camera to catch the killers within 48 hours.
By now, more than 127,000 hours have passed. Yet, agency after agency tasked by the government with investigating the murder has failed to produce a probe report.
The Sagar-Runi murder case now holds the record for the highest number of court hearing deferrals due to the non-submission of an investigation report, having been officially postponed 129 times.
While the Guinness World Records does not officially track this category, legal experts, human rights organizations, and media outlets widely cite it as an unprecedented anomaly in global judicial history.
This agonizing wait for justice has seen the couple’s minor son grow into an adult, traumatized by the fact that the killers remain unknown after 14 years.
Sagar Sarowar, a news editor for Maasranga Television, and his wife Meherun Runi, a senior reporter at ATN Bangla, were brutally murdered in their rented flat in West Rajabazar, Dhaka, on February 11, 2012, in the presence of their four-year-old son.
Over the past 14 years, the investigation has repeatedly changed hands, moving from the Detective Branch (DB) to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), and finally to the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI). None of these shifts have yielded fruit.
Initially, the DB of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police was entrusted with the case before it was transferred to RAB. The elite crime-busting agency failed to submit its investigation report to the court, requesting extensions 111 times over 12 years.
On September 30, 2024, the High Court stripped RAB of its investigative authority. Three weeks later, the Ministry of Home Affairs formed a new high-powered task force, led by the PBI, to handle the investigation.
The High Court directed the authorities to complete the investigation and submit the report within six months, noting that the delay was a matter of regret not only for the victims' family but for every citizen. The court famously observed that "six months means six months."
The higher judiciary has previously noted that the delay in completing the investigation and commencing the trial is a continuous mockery of the justice system that damages the judiciary's reputation.
Public perception suggests that the sense of urgency and justice expressed by the higher judiciary is not reflected in the actions of the investigating agencies and government functionaries.
Requesting fresh extensions has become a ritualistic routine for these agencies, granting them a two-to-three-month respite before the cycle repeats.
No matter which agency takes the lead, the result remains the same: Endless delays and virtually zero new leads to pursue the perpetrators or formally begin the trial.
To break this decade-long deadlock, the High Court issued a series of binding directives. When the newly formed task force faced structural hurdles following the major political shifts in Bangladesh after August 5, 2024, the High Court granted a final six-month extension, ordering an unyielding submission.
In discussions about press gags and media intimidation in Bangladesh, the impunity surrounding this case remains a stark example of a hazardous working environment for journalists.
With an elected government now in power in post-February 2026 Bangladesh, fast-tracking this double-murder case is essential to restore faith in the country’s investigating agencies and pave the way for an intimidation-free media ecosystem.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

Addressing a press conference in Karachi, PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh said Afridi and the party’s central leadership would enter Sindh on Sept 3. The delegation would receive a major welcome at Kamoon Shaheed at 11am before travelling to different cities across the province, he said.

“The delegation, led by CM Afridi, will travel from Jacobabad to Naushehro Feroze on Sept 4, proceed from Naushehro Feroze to Hyderabad on Sept 5 and reach Karachi on Sept 6,” he announced.

Sheikh added that large gatherings linked to the party’s street movement would also be held in different cities during the tour.

“A major rally will be held on Shahrah-i-Quaideen in Karachi on Sept 6,” Sheikh said, expressing hope that the authorities would grant permission for the event. “Even if permission is not granted, there will be a rally in Karachi,” he asserted.

He said Sept 6 was Defence Day and that the PTI would speak about the defence of Pakistan and the rights of its people.

Speaking at the same press conference, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said the PTI would also observe Sept 27 as Democracy Day and protest for the release of party founder Imran Khan, and called on people to continue raising their voices for their rights.

“This is not a battle for one day; it is a question of the future of the entire nation,” he said.

Raja said the country’s poor had expressed themselves through their votes, but their mandate had been “stolen”. He claimed millions of Pakistanis had voted for Imran on Feb 8, 2024, in the hope of determining their future, but their mandate was subsequently denied.

He also claimed that PTI candidates had won 21 of the 22 National Assembly seats in Karachi, while seats won by the party in Lahore and elsewhere had also been “taken away”.

Referring to reports of electoral irregularities, he alleged that the elections were marred by “worst rigging” and that candidates rejected by voters were subsequently imposed on them.

PTI Secretary General Raja said Pakistan had effectively developed two separate systems — one for the rich and another for the poor — and that the deaths of 14 newborn babies at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) had exposed the failure of a system that did not adequately protect the disadvantaged.

Expressing grief over the infants’ deaths, Raja said the tragedy had raised serious questions about the state of public healthcare. “A committee comprising those responsible has been formed, but the question is: where is the country heading?” he said.

He warned that a tragedy of this nature could occur anywhere in the country. Referring to claims that “the system had failed”, he asked which system had actually failed. “We need to fix the system that supports the poor,” he said.

Raja also said around 25 million children in Pakistan were currently out of school and that the country was wasting their potential. “Poor children are not receiving the education they deserve,” he said, adding that Pakistan had developed a degree of social and educational segregation rarely seen elsewhere, including Bangladesh.

“Pims tragedy is another manifestation of this inequality, as wealthy families generally do not depend on basic health units while poor people have no alternative,” he said.

Raja claimed that around 40 per cent of children in the country were behind in mental development for their age, leaving them disadvantaged throughout their lives.

“Imran Khan’s message is about the poor. He talks about equal education and opportunities for children of the rich and poor,” he said.

The PTI leader also alleged that people who raised their voices were being picked up, while journalists who spoke the truth were being removed from their organisations. “Journalists who used to raise their voice for the truth are unemployed today,” he said.

He said democracy had never been allowed to fully flourish in Pakistan and questioned whether the creation of new provinces would resolve the country’s political problems. Islamabad, he noted, was a small city, yet its hospitals and education system were also facing serious difficulties.

Raja further said any decision to create new provinces or alter the existing provincial structure should be taken by the people through an assembly representing their genuine mandate. He called for strengthening the local government system and devolving powers to the grassroots.

“Everyone knows how the mayor was made in Karachi,” he said, adding that no system could function if people continued to be deprived of their electoral rights.

Raja also alleged that PTI’s votes had been “stolen” in Karachi’s local government elections.

He urged people to come out and make their voices heard, assuring them that the PTI leadership would remain at the forefront of the struggle. “If 250 million people come out of their homes and onto the streets, this system will collapse,” he said.

item.title: Claims that CDF Munir visited Iran as envoy for US 'incorrect, misleading': FO. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The Foreign Office (FO) on Thursday termed claims that Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir visited Iran as an “envoy” of the United States “misleading and factually incorrect”.

The army chief met the Iranian leadership during his day-long visit to Tehran on August 24, undertaken as part of Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to end the stalemate in the ongoing US-Iran conflict. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had also accompanied him.

Addressing a weekly press briefing in Islamabad on Thursday, FO Spokesperson Tahir Andrabi noted that the discussions held during CDF Munir’s visit to Tehran “focused on regional de-escalation, breaking the military stalemate and exploring a negotiated settlement to restore peace and stability”.

“I will also highlight that claims by certain quarters that the COAS and CDF visited Iran as envoy of President Trump or the US are misleading and factually incorrect, as his visit was undertaken purely in the context and backdrop of Pakistan’s role as a mediator,” he said.

Andrabi asserted that the visit underscored Islamabad’s “sincere and constructive role in bridging the difference between Washington and Tehran”. He noted that the Iranian leadership appreciated Pakistan’s efforts towards de-escalation and peaceful resolution of the conflict.

He stressed that Pakistan “remains engaged alongside our brotherly countries in sincere and concerted efforts towards resolving the crises in the Middle East and Gulf and with respect to the standoff between the US and Iran”.

“Pakistan will continue to actively pursue diplomatic engagement and support all sincere efforts aimed at reviving the peace talks and achieving a comprehensive, just and lasting resolution of the conflict,” he said.

Asked for a comment on the recent US plans for expansion of sanctions on countries doing business with Iran, Andrabi said Pakistan was “following international law and our bilateral trade agreements with Iran”.

“As such, our trade remains in consonance with our obligations,” he affirmed.

Asked about the US’s “economic war” against Iran, Andrabi expressed Islamabad’s hope that “all economic issues will also be settled in the long run” as part of a wider settlement of the US-Iran standoff.

Besides the CDF’s visit, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also remained engaged with his counterparts on regional developments, Andrabi pointed out. He added that over the past two weeks, Dar spoke with Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan three times.

A Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in mid-June provided for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and left it up to Tehran and Muscat “to define the future administration and maritime services” in the waterway, in discussion with Gulf states and in line with international law.

But the deal, which was supposed to pave the way for talks on permanently ending the war, has since fallen apart.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi visited Tehran on Tuesday, where he discussed a framework agreement that would establish a “temporary corridor” for shipping and a project to clear mines in the strait.

Although there has been no clear breakthrough yet, and fundamental differences persist between Iran and the US, the latest diplomatic activity has brought the political and technical dimensions of the dispute back into focus.

The Iranian position, nevertheless, remains conditional as it continues to regard the Islamabad MoU as the appropriate framework, but wants Washington to demonstrate through concrete action that it is prepared to honour its commitments.

‘Tangible actions’ needed from Kabul rather than mere assurances: FO

Responding to a query on Afghan Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani’s reported remarks on a proposed security mechanism, Andrabi said: “Pakistan notes the proposal by the interim Afghan government’s interior minister for a dedicated mechanism to address contentious issues.

“We remain open to state-level dialogue. However, the sustainability of any mechanism will depend on tangible actions rather than mere assurances.”

The FO spokesperson emphasised that for any dialogue to take place, the Afghan Taliban must ensure that Afghan soil is not used to perpetrate terrorism against Pakistan.

“Kabul must honour its international commitments, including those under the Doha framework and ensure that Afghan soil is not used by hostile proxies, particularly the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan and the Baloch Liberation Army, against Pakistan,” he said.

Andrabi reiterated that Islamabad remained ready for “institutional coordination provided it results in tangible and verifiable counterterrorism measures and effective border management”.

In the past few years, Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

FO rejects former Indian defence chief’s claims regarding 2025 conflict

Replying to another question, the FO spokesperson rubbished claims made by India’s ex-defence chief, Anil Chauhan, that an Indian Harop drone accidentally struck Kirana Hills near Sargodha during the May 2025 conflict after running critically low on fuel.

“We categorically reject the self-contradictory and retrospective claims made by the former Indian chief of defence staff regarding Kirana Hills,” Andrabi maintained.

He asserted that during the conflict, “Pakistan’s layered air defence network effectively thwarted India’s military objectives, while Pakistan’s subsequent response under Operation Bunyanum Marsoos demonstrated our ability to impose cost across the conflict spectrum”.

“No strategic asset or sensitive infrastructure was compromised in Pakistan. Attempts to retrospectively recast these events through selective narrative or dramatised production cannot alter the verifiable operational record of May 2025,” he said.

The FO spokesperson said that history is “established by facts and evidence, not by Bollywood-style retrospective claims”.

“These post-facto punches, if I may call them, 16 or 17 months after the war would be better directed at their faces,” he added.

Regarding a question about the removal of the structures outside Pakistan’s High Commission in New Delhi, Andrabi said Islamabad has “launched a strong protest” and termed the act a violation of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

The FO spokesperson noted that Indian “authorities used heavy machinery to demolish sheds, benches, and a walkway adjacent to the consular section” of the High Commission. He added that the facility was used by those seeking consular assistance and visas.

He pointed out that Indian actions against Pakistan’s High Commission in New Delhi were initiated “without prior notice, and therefore cannot be equated with the actions here in Islamabad”.

“Any attempt to link this incident to Islamabad’s ongoing non-discriminatory anti-encroachment drive in the Diplomatic Enclave is misleading,” Andrabi stated, noting that a notification was given to the Indian side but it “failed to remove such structures”.

He stressed that the drive “targets unauthorised structures outside all diplomatic missions, not just India, in the Diplomatic Enclave”.

Makkah pact an ‘evolving security architecture’

Asked about Bangladesh’s interest in joining the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the FO spokesperson said: “As an evolving security architecture, the MJDA remains open to countries who share their commitments to collective obligations and common security interests.”

The joint defence agreement signed on August 7 aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

Andrabi stressed that the pact is a “defensive framework aimed at safeguarding peace and promoting regional stability”.

He added that any formal request by another country to join the pact will be considered in consultation with Riyadh and Ankara.

“The operationalisation of the MJDA, however, remains at an early stage,” he said.

How lawful was the appointment of the chairman of the ACC?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On August 17, pursuant to an order of the President, the Cabinet Secretary issued a notification appointing Justice (Retd) AKM Asaduzzaman as the chairman of the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). Many people have expressed opinions for and against the appointment on social media, and questions have been raised as to whether the appointment is legally valid.
Bangladesh exercises its constitutional supremacy. Article 99(1) deals with the disabilities of the judges after retirement. It says, "a person who has held office as a judge (otherwise than as an additional judge pursuant to the provisions of article 98), shall not, after his retirement or removal therefrom, plead or act before any court or authority or hold any office of profit in the service of the republic not being a judicial or quasi-judicial office.”
Let us pay particular attention to the latter part. It clearly states that such a person shall not be eligible for appointment to any office of profit in the service of the republic. However, he or she may be appointed to a judicial or quasi-judicial office.
This provision raises several questions. First, do the duties and functions of the chairman of the ACC fall within the “service of the republic”? Second, is the position an “office of profit?” And finally, is the ACC a judicial or quasi-judicial institution?
Article 152 of the Constitution defines the term “the service of the republic” as "any service, post or office whether in a civil or military capacity, in respect of the government of Bangladesh, and any other service declared by law to be a service of the republic."
The next question, therefore, is whether the functions of the chairman of the ACC fall within the “service of the Republic” and whether the position constitutes an office of profit. To find the answer, it is necessary to take a look at the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. Under section 2(b) of the Act, the chairman and every other commissioner of the commission are collectively referred to as “commissioner.”
At this point, reference should be made to a judgment of the High Court Division. The court held that the ACC is an independent statutory body governed by the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, and that the functions of its commissioners constitute service of the republic and the office of commissioner is an office of profit.
The decision of the High Court Division was subsequently challenged before the Appellate Division. A Full Bench of the Appellate Division affirm the decision of the High Court Division. The Appellate Division, most importantly, also made no exception regarding the office or functions of the chairman.
Since, under the ACC Act, the chairman is also deemed to be a commissioner, and since the decision reported does not distinguish the chairman from the other commissioners or create any exception in this regard, every word of that decision is equally applicable to the chairman.
In other words, the office of chairman of the ACC is an office of profit in the service of the republic, and the functions performed by the chairman constitute service of the republic.
Now let us turn to the final question: Is the ACC a judicial or quasi-judicial institution?
To answer this question, we must first understand what is meant by “judicial” and “quasi-judicial.”
Neither the Constitution of Bangladesh nor any other prevailing law provides a specific definition of these two terms.
However, an analysis of the judicial and administrative structures gives us a basic understanding of the concepts. Whether an institution is judicial or quasi-judicial depends, among other things, on whether it possesses the authority to adjudicate matters.
Under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, the ACC may receive complaints, conduct inquiries and investigations, exercise powers of arrest in cases provided by law, and even conduct hearings.
However, the power to investigate, inquire, arrest or conduct a hearing is not the same as judicial power. The ACC does not have the authority to finally adjudicate an allegation and deliver a judgment. Therefore, the ACC cannot, in any sense, be regarded as a judicial institution.
Then, is the ACC a quasi-judicial institution? Neither the ACC Act nor its rules expressly characterize the commission as quasi-judicial. Therefore, unless the Supreme Court provides a different interpretation, there appears to be little scope for treating the ACC as a quasi-judicial institution.
Furthermore, section 5 of the ACC Act expressly provides that, whether the appointment is valid or not, no question may be raised regarding the validity of any act done by the chairman while holding office.
On the other hand, Article 134 of the Constitution provides that, except as otherwise provided by the Constitution, every individual in the service of the republic shall remain in office so long as the President so desires.
Therefore, the office of the ACC chairman, the tenure of the office, and the constitutional role of the President all require consideration together.
Thus, the appointment of the chairman of the ACC is not merely a matter of political controversy; it is also an important question of constitutional and legal interpretation.
If the ACC is neither a judicial nor a quasi-judicial institution, and if the office of chairman is regarded as an office of profit in the service of the republic, then it is only natural to question whether the appointment of a retired Supreme Court judge to that position is compatible with Article 99(1) of the Constitution.
For the past 17 years, the fallen authoritarian government gradually turned each and every sector of the state into an instrument of fascism, not merely crippling the state machinery but effectively crushing it under the weight of fascism.
Restoring the country and the state from such a fragile condition is a major challenge for this government.
It is a political culture of this subcontinent that governments appoint persons of their choice to important positions in important institutions. Moreover, since every human being is political to some extent, it is natural that an appointee may have a political ideology.
But appointments must be made on the basis of competence. Appointments must be transparent, lawful, and valid.
If an opportunity arises to question the legality of an appointment made by a government formed with the mandate of the people, it is natural that doubts may arise in the public mind regarding the government's belief in and sincerity toward its slogan: “Bangladesh first.”
I hope and believe that this government will move toward a balanced and lawful resolution of this complex situation involving law, politics, and bureaucracy.
Because, ultimately, the state is greater than any individual; institutions are greater than any position or rank.
Saffat Homayra is an Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

Dengue is not slowing down. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dengue has long evolved from a seasonal spike into one of Bangladesh’s most persistent and deadly public health threats.
It is indeed truly unfortunate that, instead of eliminating this disease that ought to be fully preventable, we have now normalized daily deaths as a result of it.
Dengue has become a year‑round danger, and beyond the tragedy of lives lost every day, it is our entire healthcare apparatus that suffers greatly. Hospitals fill up as families scramble for care, all the while preventable deaths continue to rise.
The pattern is painfully familiar, and yet the response remains largely reactive.
Emergency measures are only taken once hospitals are overwhelmed, and it is a frustrating cycle that cannot continue.
Without structural fixes, no amount of fogging or awareness campaigns will be enough. City corporations must treat vector control as a year‑long responsibility, not a monsoon ritual.
Public awareness also needs to evolve. Dengue is not “just another fever” but one that kills and devastates families daily.
Bangladesh must also strengthen hospital preparedness. Every year, the same story repeats: Shortages of beds, testing kits, and trained staff. A country that knows dengue will return annually has no excuse for being caught unprepared.
The daily deaths must be a reminder that dengue is not to be taken lightly. It is a test of governance, coordination, and political seriousness. Lives are being lost - today, yesterday, and tomorrow - because the response is still not matching the scale of the threat.
We must act decisively, consistently, and with the understanding that dengue is no longer a seasonal inconvenience. It is a national crisis that requires full attention and commitment to combating it.

item.title: Being transparent during times of crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is no denying the fact that our country, ever since the Israel-US attack on Iran, has been affected and is presently suffering from a shortage of power and fuel.
There has been extensive coverage about how the energy crisis has forced numerous factories to halt production as fuel and power become unreliable. There has also been equal coverage regarding people’s woes with load shedding, cooking gas, and a lack of CNG for vehicles.
To this end, those within the government not taking responsibility, and suggesting that all is well, is not helpful.
While it may be factually correct to state that we are on the path to correcting these issues, there is a troubling gap between official messaging and the lived reality of businesses, workers, and the general population that we struggle to reconcile.
Governance depends on trust, and trust is built on candour and verifiable data. Unfortunately, this remains an area where we remain woefully inadequate.
The remedy is and has always been straightforward. The least the authorities can do is publish granular, timely figures and explain anomalies when they occur.
If increased supply is indeed being absorbed by rising residential demand, maintenance outages, contractual constraints, or price distortions that divert fuel from industry, say so and outline corrective steps. If distribution failures or affordability, rather than absolute scarcity, are the problem, policy responses must follow that diagnosis.
This should not be too much to ask.
Practical measures should include a transparent reporting dashboard, a rapid‑response channel for businesses to log outages, and short‑term relief for labour‑intensive manufacturers while longer reforms proceed.
Predictable energy underpins jobs, exports, and livelihoods for the entirety of the country. Spin and silence will only deepen economic pain and erode confidence.
Our leaders must therefore tell the whole story - honestly, promptly, and with the evidence to back it up - so that everyone in the country can move from confusion to coordinated action to best approach these challenging times.

item.title: The clock is ticking on Bangladesh’s demographic dividend. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is a quiet countdown unfolding in Bangladesh. Unlike election calendars or development plans, this clock cannot be extended by political promises or bureaucratic delays. It is the demographic clock.
For a few precious years, Bangladesh enjoys a rare advantage that many developed nations now desperately wish they still possessed: A predominantly young population capable of powering extraordinary economic transformation.
Yet demographic dividends are never guaranteed. They are earned. If neglected, they quietly expire, leaving behind frustrated generations and unrealized dreams.
The country’s public conversation often celebrates youth as Bangladesh’s greatest asset. The phrase has become almost ceremonial, repeated in policy documents, speeches, and development reports.
But an asset that remains idle gradually transforms into a liability. Human potential follows the same economic logic. When millions of educated young people cannot find meaningful work, their disappointment becomes more than an individual tragedy. It slowly erodes productivity, social trust, and confidence in institutions.
Recent findings from the United Nations Population Fund capture this growing unease. More than two-thirds of Bangladeshi youth worry about their future economic security. This anxiety deserves attention because it reflects something deeper than unemployment statistics. It reveals a generation uncertain whether education still guarantees opportunity or whether hard work can genuinely improve their lives.
Bangladesh has not failed to produce graduates. Universities, colleges, and private institutions continue to send thousands of degree holders into the labour market every year.
The real crisis lies elsewhere. The country has become remarkably efficient at producing credentials while remaining comparatively ineffective at producing employable capabilities. Diplomas have multiplied faster than practical competencies.
This disconnect explains a paradox that has become increasingly visible. Employers regularly complain about shortages of skilled workers while educated job seekers struggle to secure employment.
The World Bank estimates that although approximately 14 million young people entered Bangladesh’s labour market over the past decade, only around 8.7 million found employment. Meanwhile, official statistics indicate that millions remain underemployed or work in positions far below their qualifications. A considerable share of them possess university degrees.
This mismatch is not merely an educational problem. It exposes a structural weakness in the country’s development model. Educational institutions often design curricula with limited consultation from industries that will eventually employ graduates.
Employers seek adaptability, digital literacy, communication, teamwork, analytical thinking, and practical experience. Many graduates arrive with theoretical knowledge but limited exposure to solving real-world problems.
The consequence is predictable. Businesses invest additional time and resources in retraining employees while countless qualified applicants remain excluded from opportunities.
Ironically, Bangladesh’s economic success has made this challenge more visible.
As industries become more technologically sophisticated, they require increasingly specialized skills. Traditional manufacturing alone can no longer absorb the growing youth population.
Emerging sectors such as information technology, advanced manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, renewable energy, financial technology, and digital services demand workers capable of continuous learning rather than static expertise.
The discussion around unemployment often overlooks another uncomfortable reality. Employment alone is no longer an adequate indicator of progress. The quality of employment matters just as much as its quantity.
Many young Bangladeshis have embraced entrepreneurship and self-employment, often celebrated as evidence of resilience. Their determination deserves recognition.
Yet necessity-driven entrepreneurship differs fundamentally from opportunity-driven entrepreneurship. Too many young people establish tiny businesses not because they discovered innovative market opportunities but because formal employment remained inaccessible.
These enterprises frequently operate with limited technology, inadequate financing, weak market access, and little managerial support. They create livelihoods but rarely generate sustained productivity gains or large-scale employment for others.
This distinction matters because demographic dividends depend not simply on keeping people occupied but on maximizing their productive contribution. A country where millions survive through low-productivity activities cannot fully capitalize on its youthful population, regardless of employment statistics.
Equally concerning is the country’s fragmented approach to skill development. Various ministries, agencies, and development partners conduct thousands of training programs annually. Training centres continue expanding, certificates continue accumulating, and projects continue receiving funding.
Yet surprisingly little public attention focuses on outcomes. How many trainees actually secure relevant employment? How much do their incomes increase? Which programs genuinely respond to changing labour market demands?
Without rigorous evaluation, training risks becoming another administrative exercise measured byenrollment rather than impact.
International migration presents another revealing example of missed opportunity. Bangladesh remains one of the world’s leading labour-exporting countries, sending hundreds of thousands of workers abroad each year. Remittances have become a pillar of economic stability.
Yet the overwhelming majority of migrant workers continue occupying relatively low-skilled positions. Consequently, their earnings remain limited despite significant personal sacrifice.
This becomes particularly significant when observing demographic changes elsewhere. Countries facing rapidly ageing populations increasingly seek technically skilled and linguistically prepared foreign workers.
Japan, for example, requires healthcare professionals, technicians, engineers, and caregivers equipped with specialized competencies and language proficiency. Bangladesh possesses abundant human resources but often lacks the preparation needed to access these higher-paying opportunities. The gap is not demographic. It is developmental.
Meanwhile, technological disruption continues accelerating. Artificial intelligence, automation, robotics, and digital platforms are redefining occupations across every sector.
Entire professions are evolving faster than educational systems can revise textbooks. The most valuable workers tomorrow may not necessarily be those possessing the most information but those capable of learning, adapting, collaborating, and solving unfamiliar problems.
Unfortunately, Bangladesh’s educational culture still rewards memorization more consistently than creativity. Technical and vocational education continues carrying unnecessary social stigma despite offering some of the strongest employment prospects.
Parents frequently encourage university degrees regardless of market demand while vocational pathways remain undervalued. Society celebrates certificates more enthusiastically than competencies.
This mindset requires urgent reconsideration. Countries that successfully transformed demographic advantages into sustained prosperity invested not only in expanding education but also in aligning education with economic strategy. Their classrooms communicated constantly with factories, laboratories, technology firms, hospitals, and export industries. Skills evolved alongside markets instead of lagging behind them.
None of this diminishes the government’s responsibility to strengthen policies. Nor does it reduce the importance of private sector investment, industrial expansion, or regulatory reform.
On the contrary, demographic dividends emerge only when education, industry, finance, innovation, infrastructure, and governance reinforce one another. No ministry can achieve this transformation independently.
Bangladesh still possesses time, but considerably less than public discourse often assumes. Demographic opportunities resemble favourable weather for agriculture. Farmers cannot postpone planting until the season feels more convenient. Once the window closes, no amount of later effort can recover the lost harvest.
The country’s greatest economic challenge therefore is not simply creating more jobs or offering more training. It is ensuring that every young Bangladeshi acquires capabilities matching an economy that does not yet fully exist but is rapidly approaching.
The future will reward countries that prepare workers before industries mature rather than after opportunities disappear. Bangladesh’s demographic dividend ultimately depends less on the size of its youth population than on whether today’s generation becomes tomorrow’s competitive advantage instead of tomorrow’s greatest regret.
HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT. He can be reached at nazmulalam.rijohn@gmail.com .
